findings.short_summary: --benchmark-skip grep assertion can never fail
findings.summary: The `--benchmark-skip` half of `test_the_latency_gate_is_still_armed` cannot fail: `pyproject.toml` line 55 is a comment that begins `# --benchmark-skip:`, so the substring survives deletion of the flag from `addopts`.
findings.failure_scenario: Verified: `sed '59s/ --benchmark-skip//' pyproject.toml | grep -c -- '--benchmark-skip'` returns 1 — the comment at pyproject.toml:55 ("# --benchmark-skip: the perf-benchmark suite (tests/test_perf_benchmarks.py) / only runs when explicitly requested via --benchmark-only...") keeps the string alive. Someone removes `--benchmark-skip` from `addopts` (line 59); every ordinary `uv run pytest` then runs the six timed latency benchmarks, and the test whose docstring says it guards "the `--benchmark-skip` default that keeps these benchmarks off an ordinary `pytest` run" stays green. Directly against CLAUDE.md:113-125: "The bar is 'would this test FAIL if the code under test were broken?' — if not, it isn't a test." (The sibling assertion on line 513 is sound: `--benchmark-compare-fail=min:15%` appears exactly once in ci.yml, in the run command at :72, with no comment mentioning it.)

import tomllib
    addopts = tomllib.loads((root / "pyproject.toml").read_text())["tool"]["pytest"]["ini_options"]["addopts"]
    assert "--benchmark-skip" in addopts

findings.short_summary: 548-day oracle corpus is one shape, 548 times
findings.summary: The equivalence oracle's anti-vacuity floor (`assert len(by_date) > 500`) presents a 548-day corpus that is measurably one input shape repeated 548 times, and neither it nor the six edge cases contains a multi-activity day — the exact case the fold changed.
findings.failure_scenario: Measured against the real fixture (scripts/perf_fixture.py:196-206 seeds one row per date, always `activity_type='running'`, always with no `avg_pace_sec_per_km`): 548 days, max 1 activity/day, exactly 1 distinct classification shape `(('running', paceless, dist>0),)`, and every single day returns `['running']`. The `walking` branch, the `other` branch and every multi-activity list are never differentially compared. The fold's actual control-flow change is that `classes.add('other')` now runs inside the loop that accumulates `foot`/`dur` and hits `continue` before the distance work — so a day holding one on-foot activity and one ride is the case that would catch an ordering or accumulation mistake, and no case in `_WORKOUT_ACTUALS_EDGE_CASES` (all six are single-activity) or in the 548-day loop is one. Combined with `test_workout_actuals_evaluates_ran_once_per_on_foot_activity` (:269), which passes a mixed 3-activity day but asserts only the `_ran` count and never the returned classes, the mixed-day fold is differentially untested here; only `tests/test_plans.py:test_workout_actuals_returns_foot_run_and_walk_in_one_pass` covers it, and it is not an oracle against the pre-fold implementation. Same CLAUDE.md rule as above ("never coverage theater", :113-125) plus its "Cover the edge cases" clause.
findings.suggestion: Add a mixed day to `_WORKOUT_ACTUALS_EDGE_CASES`, e.g. `[_PACED_RUN, _PACED_WALK, _RIDE, {"activity_type": None, "distance_meters": 100.0}]`, and assert a floor on `len(_WORKOUT_ACTUALS_EDGE_CASES)` the way `_ROUND_FLOATS_CASES` does at :506.

findings.short_summary: Docstring says bool guard is now load-bearing; it isn't
findings.summary: The new docstring parenthetical claims the `bool` guard "becomes load-bearing" under the fast path and forbids any test showing otherwise; measured, the guard is still completely inert after this change.
findings.failure_scenario: Deleted `if isinstance(obj, bool): return obj` (tools.py:187-188) from the post-change implementation and differentially fuzzed it against the pre-inline reference over 40,000 randomly generated nested payloads (dicts/lists/dict-subclass/list-subclass containers; leaves covering float, float/int subclasses, bool, int, str, None, NaN, +/-inf, -0.0, tuple, bytes, Decimal, date, frozenset, OrderedDict; high-precision and non-string keys), comparing structurally with type preservation, not via json.dumps: 0 divergences — identical to the 0 divergences the unmodified new implementation produces. The reason is that the guard was never reachable in a way that mattered and still isn't: both container fast paths copy a `bool` child inline via `t is bool` (lines 199, 211) and never recurse for it, and the fallback `isinstance` ladder (lines 220-225) still has no `int` branch, so a bool arriving at the top falls all the way through to `return obj` unchanged. There is no `int` fast path that rounds — line 199/211 only copy. Cost: the comment states a false invariant about the code three lines below it, and instructs the next author ("no test may claim removing it is observable") on the strength of that false reason, so the guard's real status — dead-but-harmless defensive code — is now recorded backwards in the one place a reader checks.

findings.short_summary: Third axis is skipped by the only run the docstring names
findings.summary: The new third axis never runs in the invocation this file's own docstring says is the only one that runs it — `--benchmark-only` skips every non-benchmark test, so all six new tests are skipped in CI's perf-gate step.
findings.failure_scenario: Ran it: `pytest tests/test_perf_benchmarks.py --benchmark-only` reports `6 passed, 16 skipped` with `SKIPPED [16] Skipping non-benchmark (--benchmark-only active).` — pytest-benchmark's `pytest_collection_modifyitems` (plugin.py:336-347) marks every item without the `benchmark` fixture skipped under `--benchmark-only`. `.github/workflows/ci.yml:70` is exactly that invocation, so the entire work-COUNT axis and both equivalence oracles are skipped in the "Perf-benchmark regression gate" step and only execute in the "Run tests with coverage gate" step. Lines 4-7 of this same docstring — unchanged by the diff — say "a plain `uv run pytest` never runs the ... benchmarks here — only an explicit `--benchmark-only` invocation does", and the diff appends "Three axes are asserted" under it. A maintainer debugging a red perf gate reads that header, expects the work counts to be part of what the gate reported, and will not find them; a maintainer adding a fourth work-count assertion will reasonably put it behind the `benchmark` fixture and silently disable it in the coverage job instead. The axis does run in CI (in the other step), so this is a documentation/placement defect, not dead code.

findings.summary: The PR adds a third assertion axis to the perf suite and edits the same CLAUDE.md bullet, but leaves that bullet's description of what the suite asserts at "latency AND `db.connect()`-open-count".
findings.failure_scenario: CLAUDE.md:234-239 states the rule verbatim: "**Keep CLAUDE.md current — in the same commit/PR.** Any change that alters the workflow, architecture, deploy/branch model, security contract, or an env var updates the relevant CLAUDE.md section as part of that same commit, not as a follow-up. CLAUDE.md is the source of truth future-you reads first; a diff that changes behavior but leaves CLAUDE.md stale is incomplete." The diff edits lines 199-221 of this very bullet (adding drift-tell part 3) and updates the test module docstring from "Two axes are asserted" to "Three axes are asserted", yet CLAUDE.md:160-161 still reads "separate axis from the coverage gate: latency AND `db.connect()`-open-count for the brief/plan hot paths". findings.short_summary: json.dumps oracle can't see tuple vs list
findings.summary: `_dumped`'s `json.dumps` comparison is type-blind, so the oracle cannot assert the tuple-to-list conversion the cases at :412 and :413 exist to cover, nor any container/scalar subclass identity.
findings.failure_scenario: `json.dumps((1.23, 2.35)) == json.dumps([1.23, 2.35]) == '[1.23, 2.35]'`, and `default=str` further collapses anything unserializable to its `str()`. The approved plan's Proof 5 names "a `tuple` (must become a `list`)" as a required case and `_ROUND_FLOATS_CASES` duly carries `(1.23456789, 2.3456789)` and `[(1.23456789,), (2.3456789,)]` — but the comparison function cannot distinguish pass from fail on that property. A later fast-path extension such as `if type(obj) is tuple: return obj` (a tempting next optimization, since tuples currently take the slow ladder) changes `_round_floats`'s return type contract and leaves both oracle tests green. The same blindness covers `_FloatSubclass`/`_IntSubclass`/`_DictSubclass`: `_mishandles_a_dict_subclass` only diverges because its *values* stay unrounded, not because its type differs, so the two-sidedness proof at :463 does not demonstrate type coverage either. (For the record, a type-preserving 40k-case differential fuzz confirms the shipped implementation IS equivalent today — the gap is that the committed oracle would not notice if it stopped being.)
findings.suggestion: Compare with a type-preserving normalizer, or add one direct assertion: `assert isinstance(tools._round_floats((1.0, 2.0)), list)`.
findings.head: 776ccbd5cb96c9d46946418b037241eaa1623d51

findings.short_summary: grade_workout re-walks the day list just walked
findings.summary: The fold removes one redundant pass over the day's activity list but leaves another in the same caller loop: `classify_workout` recomputes `_running_distance`/`_foot_distance`, values `_workout_actuals` returned two lines earlier.
findings.failure_scenario: In `build_plan_detail` (plans.py:1254-1257) each iteration calls `_workout_actuals(day, cfg)` — which returns `foot` and `run_m` — and then immediately `grade_workout(w, day, frontier, cfg)`, whose `classify_workout` recomputes `_foot_distance(day_activities)` (plans.py:337) or `_running_distance(day_activities, cfg)` (plans.py:339) or `_running_duration(day_activities, cfg)` (plans.py:351) over the same list, evaluating `_ran` once more per activity. Because `_ran` checks on-foot first (plans.py:165-166, "ON-FOOT IS CHECKED FIRST"), `_running_distance(day, cfg)` is exactly the `run_m` already in hand and `_foot_distance(day)` is exactly `foot` — the recomputation is byte-identical work. Measured on the perf fixture at this head: the handler still makes 87 `_ran` calls (and 83 `_round_floats` calls) for one `get_training_plan_progress` request; the fold's own accounting (one `_ran` per on-foot activity) implies roughly a third of that. Cheaper alternative: have `_workout_actuals` also accumulate running duration and pass its five/six-tuple into `grade_workout`/`classify_workout` instead of letting them re-derive it. This predates the diff, but the diff's new docstring sentence on this very line — "Anything else this day needs is computed in the loop below, not in a pass of its own" — is contradicted by the next statement in its only caller, so the invariant it re-asserts is still not true at the handler level.

findings.short_summary: Progress payload rebuilt per test instead of once
findings.summary: `_capture_progress_payload` re-runs the whole `get_training_plan_progress` handler over the 3-year fixture once per calling test, for a payload that is identical both times.
findings.failure_scenario: Cost: the new block adds four full `get_training_plan_progress.handler({})` invocations to the ordinary `pytest` job — one each in `test_get_training_plan_progress_does_not_double_classify` (:279) and `test_get_training_plan_progress_rounds_without_a_call_per_node` (:287), which genuinely need their own counted run, plus one each in `test_round_floats_output_is_identical_to_the_pre_inline_implementation` (:449) and `test_the_round_floats_oracle_can_actually_fail` (:463), which both want the same unchanging payload object. During capture the handler also runs with `_round_floats` wrapped, so every node pays two Python frames instead of one. Cheaper alternative: make the captured payload a module-scoped fixture (built once alongside `perf_db`) and have both oracle tests consume it, removing one full handler run and one wrapped traversal from every suite run — the suite CLAUDE.md:126 tells you to run before claiming done.

findings.short_summary: bool-guard rationale is false and self-contradictory
findings.summary: The new docstring claims the `int` fast path makes the top-level `bool` guard load-bearing; it does not, and the diff's own test comment says the opposite.
findings.failure_scenario: The added parenthetical says "there is no ``int`` branch there and ``isinstance(True, float)`` is False — but the ``int`` fast path below makes it load-bearing". It does not: the container fast paths match `t is bool` (tools.py:199, :211) before any recursion, and even with that arm deleted a bool never satisfies `t is int` because `type(True) is bool`, so a bool still falls to the ladder and still returns unchanged. Verified empirically at the head commit: deleting `if isinstance(obj, bool): return obj` (tools.py:187) produces byte-identical output over the real `get_training_plan_progress` payload and every case in `_ROUND_FLOATS_CASES`, plus bools nested in dicts, lists, tuples and dict subclasses. The diff's own test at tests/test_perf_benchmarks.py:470 asserts the contrary of the docstring ("removing the `bool` guard diverges on nothing"), so the two halves of one change disagree. Concrete cost: a maintainer who later adds a genuine `int` branch to the ladder will read this docstring as saying the guard already protects that case and will not add the test that would catch `True` serializing as `1`.

(Against the ladder alone that guard is inert — there is no ``int`` branch

findings.short_summary: grade_workout still re-walks the same day's activities
findings.summary: The fold removes only 36 of the handler's 87 `_ran` evaluations; the other 51 come from `grade_workout` re-walking the very same day list three more times in the same loop iteration, which is the identical defect class the diff was sent to fix.
findings.failure_scenario: Measured at the head commit against the perf fixture (`build_perf_fixture_db(today=2026-07-09)`), one `get_training_plan_progress` request: `_ran` is evaluated 87 times, of which only 36 come from `_workout_actuals` (one per activity — the fold works) and 51 come from the generator expressions in `_running_distance` (plans.py:189), `_walking_distance` and `_running_duration` (plans.py:213), reached through `grade_workout` on line 1259 — over the *same* `day` list that line 1256 just walked, in the same loop iteration. `weekly_mileage` (plans.py:1279, via the `dist_fn` at plans.py:532) walks them a fourth time. `_workout_actuals` already returns `foot`, `run` and `walk` and already accumulates `dur`, so `grade_workout` is recomputing values its caller is holding. The simpler, more general change is to hand `grade_workout` the actuals tuple `_workout_actuals` just produced (or return `dur` alongside it) instead of letting it re-derive them — that removes 51 of the 87 remaining evaluations and three list walks per graded day, versus the 36 this diff removes. As shipped, the new gate at tests/test_perf_benchmarks.py:284 pins `<= 90`, which cements the remaining duplication as the accepted floor, and `_workout_actuals`'s docstring keeps claiming "ONE pass ... `_ran` is evaluated at most once per activity" while the request as a whole evaluates it 2.4x per activity.
findings.head: 776ccbd5cb96c9d46946418b037241eaa1623d51

findings.short_summary: _ran redoes the _is_on_foot check the loop just did
findings.summary: Inside the loop this diff rewrote, `_ran(a, cfg)` re-runs the `_is_on_foot` substring scan that the line above already computed, so the loop does more label-matching work than the `_ran` count it optimises.
findings.failure_scenario: plans.py:1222 computes `_is_on_foot(at)` and `continue`s when it is False; line 1231 then calls `_ran(a, cfg)`, whose first statement (plans.py:167-169) is `if not _is_on_foot(at): return False` — the identical call on the identical value. Measured at the head commit on the perf fixture, one `get_training_plan_progress` request over 36 activities: `_is_on_foot` 139 calls and `_is_running` 226 calls, against 87 `_ran` calls. `_is_running`/`_is_walking` each lowercase the label and run an `any(...)` substring scan over a frozenset, so this is strictly more work per activity than the `_ran` dispatch the diff counts — and the new assertion counts `_ran` only, so the duplication is invisible to the gate the change adds. The deeper fix in the lines the diff already touches: split `_ran` into an on-foot-known variant (or hoist `at.lower()` once per activity) so the loop's known-on-foot branch does not pay for the check a second time. Cleanup, not a crash.
findings.head: 776ccbd5cb96c9d46946418b037241eaa1623d51

findings.short_summary: _ran count assertion has no anti-vacuity floor
findings.summary: The `_ran` work-count assertion is an upper bound with no floor, so it passes over zero work if the fixture ever stops producing an active plan.
findings.failure_scenario: `get_training_plan_progress` short-circuits at tools.py:3764 — `if active is None: return _text({"active": False})` — before any grading runs. If `plans.get_active_plan` ever stops matching the fixture's plan (a `status` value renamed, a schema migration, a change to `scripts/perf_fixture.py`'s `_seed_plan`, or the plan's date window moving out of range), `_ran` is called 0 times, `assert counts["n"] <= 90` passes, and the assertion the whole PR is built on measures nothing while still reporting green — the exact failure mode the change's own CHANGELOG entry says the latency axis suffered from for five weeks. findings.short_summary: capture wrapper fires on all 83 recursive calls
findings.summary: `_capture_progress_payload`'s wrapper is installed on the module attribute, so `captured.setdefault` runs on every recursive call, and the helper re-runs the whole handler once per test.
findings.failure_scenario: Cost: the docstring says 'The first `_round_floats` call of the handler IS the whole payload', which is true — but because the real implementation recurses through the patched module global, `capturing` is entered 83 times per handler call and does a redundant `setdefault` 82 of them. It also means the helper is silently coupled to the recursion strategy it is measuring: if `_round_floats` ever stopped recursing through the module attribute, the capture would still work but the two work-count tests above would start reading 1. Two tests each pay a full `get_training_plan_progress` run for a payload that could be captured once by a module-scoped fixture and shared. Simpler: capture with an explicit `if "payload" not in captured` and hoist the whole thing to a fixture.
